After months of on-again, off-again fighting, the United States hasn’t struck Iran in several weeks. The stretch of relative tranquility is coinciding with the final phase of the midterm-election campaign, and the assumption has been that President Trump will want to keep it going through November 3 so as not to remind voters of an unpopular war that is dragging Republican candidates down nationwide.

But that may not be what happens. The White House has asked the Pentagon to develop strike options against Iranian targets that could be exercised ahead of the midterms, according to two administration officials. The planning underscores just how much the president wants to reduce gas prices and demonstrate progress in the conflict before the vote, administration officials told us.

The size and targets of the potential strikes—and whether the administration will ultimately proceed—are still being debated. The plans are being developed by U.S. Central Command, which is coordinating the war effort, a U.S. official told us. Even the plans’ advocates acknowledge that limited strikes would not, by themselves, bring Iran to the negotiating table, restore safe travel through the Strait of Hormuz, or lower gas prices before Election Day. But those in favor believe that further action after months of uneasy peace could allow Trump to demonstrate strength and potentially declare some sort of victory, giving Republicans much-needed momentum heading into the election. “It would make the president look like he got a win and that gas prices would start going down,” a Republican familiar with the deliberations told us after being granted anonymity to discuss sensitive matters. A limited operation could be followed up by more substantial military action after the midterms, when Trump has suggested that the conflict, which is now in its eighth month, could resume.

#Gold trades 1.1% lower once again approaching key support around USD 4,100, as sellers focus on continued dollar and yield strength as well as renewed upward pressure on fuel prices. Recent selling by leveraged hedge funds continues to be partly offset by steady ETF demand, with investors seemingly seeking protection against geopolitical risks and, increasingly, concerns about the fiscal implications of persistently high borrowing costs.

The divergence is striking: US 10-year real yields have surged to an 18-year high near 3% - traditionally a major headwind for non-yielding gold - yet total ETF holdings monitored by Bloomberg have risen almost continuously since August to a four-year high of 3,145 tonnes. It suggests that, for some investors, rising yields are increasingly being viewed not only through the lens of gold’s opportunity cost, but also as a potential threat to fiscal stability and therefore a reason to maintain or increase gold exposure.

text: The relentless sell-off across global bond markets continues, with the US 10-year Treasury yield heading for a fresh 24-year closing high. In Europe, French bonds have come under renewed pressure following a brief two-day reprieve, with the 10-year yield jumping 16 basis points to 4.9%. The spread to Germany has widened to around 140 basis points, a 14-year high, highlighting mounting concerns over French fiscal stability and adding to the broader pressure on global sovereign debt markets.

El Niño continues to strengthen, with the Oceanic Niño Index (ONI) reaching 2.2°C in the latest August reading, already placing the current event firmly in the “very strong” category. By comparison, during the 2015–16 super El Niño, the index had reached around 1.7°C by August before peaking at 2.6°C in December. A similar seasonal trajectory, if maintained, would therefore point to an exceptionally strong and potentially record-breaking El Niño in the coming months.

The commodity impact is already becoming visible on both the supply and demand sides. Weather-related supply risks are supporting agricultural markets including sugar, cocoa and coffee, while a potentially milder Northern Hemisphere winter could weigh on heating demand and therefore natural gas consumption. The longer the current El Niño strengthens, the greater the risk of weather becoming a more significant commodity price driver into 2027.

#CrudeOil: Brent trades near USD 101.5 after Tuesday’s supply-led slump to USD 97 was reversed as Iran stepped up attacks on vessels attempting to cross the Strait of Hormuz. At the same time, Middle East supply continues to recover, helped by Saudi Arabia now pumping around 5.8 mb/d through its East-West pipeline. WTI continues to trade at a discount of more than USD 10 to Brent, while Brent remains heavily backwardated and gasoil trades near USD 185 per barrel, all pointing to continued tightness despite the recovery in crude supply.

Notably, ETF demand remains firm, with total holdings reaching a fresh four-year high of 3,145 tonnes, having risen by 69 tonnes during a six-week period in which the 10-year Treasury yield has surged by around 56 basis points to 5.31%. The gold-silver ratio trades near 68, where it has been pivoting for the past three months, highlighting the lack of an independent directional driver for silver beyond movements in gold.

#Wheat futures in Paris and Chicago rose for a fourth straight session as drone attacks on cargo vessels in the Black Sea raised concerns about disruption to vital grain export routes from the region. Two ships were struck on Tuesday in Bulgaria’s exclusive economic zone, including one carrying wheat from Ukraine, while another vessel was hit on Monday outside Romanian territorial waters in an attack Ukraine blamed on Russian drones. The incidents have effectively widened the high-risk area, potentially exposing commercial shipping to greater danger as soon as vessels enter the Black Sea rather than only when approaching Ukrainian ports.
